explain.say: Why can you bend a copper wire, while a stick of chalk snaps? And why do wires carry electricity? The answer is hidden in how metal atoms hold together. Look at the board, and you can follow the reasons.

explain.say: They float about! Look at the sea of electrons. These are delocalised electrons, which means not stuck to any one atom. When you connect a battery, they flow along the wire. That is electric current! Can you see now why metals conduct?

explain.say: Now look at this reason. Ions and electron sea attract each other strongly; that is the metallic bond. Push, and rows of ions slide over each other, but the sea keeps them stuck. So metals bend instead of breaking. Have you ever bent a spoon?

explain.say: Great work! Now you can compare a pure metal with an alloy, a mix of metals. Pure gold is soft because its rows slide. Add different-sized atoms, and the rows jam. Wow: that is why gold jewellery has copper mixed in, and bridges use steel, not pure iron.

faq.a: Metallic bonding is the strong attraction between positive metal ions and the sea of delocalised electrons around them.
asks: How are metal atoms held together?

faq.q: What is a sea of delocalised electrons?
faq.a: It is the outer electrons that have left the metal atoms and move freely through the whole metal. They are not attached to any one atom.

faq.q: Why can metals be bent and shaped?
faq.a: The layers of ions can slide over each other while the electron sea keeps holding them together. So metals bend instead of shattering.
An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements, like steel, which is iron with carbon. The different-sized atoms stop layers sliding, so alloys are harder.
asks: Why are alloys harder than pure metals?

faq.q: Why do metals have high melting points?
faq.a: The attraction between the ions and the electron sea is strong and acts in all directions, so lots of energy is needed to break it. Iron melts at about 1,538 °C.
asks: Why is it hard to melt metals?

facts: 22 carat gold is about 91.7 percent gold, alloyed with metals such as copper and silver to make it harder.
